slides.title: Your devices talk directly.
slides.text: No cloud in the middle. Alice's phone and Bob's laptop connect to each other, wherever they are. The layer that does this is {iroh}.

slides.title: Every device's address is a key.
slides.text: Each device has its own key pair, and its public key is its address: its {endpoint ID}. Nobody hands out addresses, and nobody can take yours.

slides.title: Finding each other.
slides.text: On the same Wi-Fi, devices simply see each other. Further away, a device publishes where it can be reached, under its own key, and anyone with the key can look it up.

slides.title: Getting through.
slides.text: Most home routers block incoming connections. iroh punches a hole from both sides at once, and usually gets a direct line. If that fails, a {relay} passes the packets along. The relay sees only sealed traffic.

slides.title: Both sides know who they talk to.
slides.text: Every connection is encrypted with the two devices' keys. Then the device shows its signer's link to an identity, so the other side knows: this is Alice's phone, acting for Alice.

slides.title: One line, three languages.
slides.text: Over one connection, devices speak a small {protocol} for each kind of work.
list: Docs: find the missing sealed chunks, then swap them.
Values: stream chunks by hash, checked as they arrive.
News: tell interested peers “there's something new”.

slides.title: Sealed chunks settle in layers.
slides.text: Every sealed change has a hash. About one in 256 hashes starts with a zero byte: that change closes a chunk holding everything since the last one. One in 65,000 starts with two zero bytes and closes a bigger chunk around the smaller ones. Like layers of {sediment}: old history ends up in a few big chunks. Every device, even a carrier that reads nothing, cuts in the same places.

slides.title: Finding what's missing, cheaply.
slides.text: Two levels. Across thousands of pieces of data, two devices exchange a few tiny mixed-up summaries and the ones that differ fall out, at about one and a half summaries per difference, however many there are. Inside one piece of data, they compare short {fingerprints} of its layers and swap exactly the missing sealed chunks, in one and a half round trips.

slides.title: A Value streams in checked chunks.
slides.text: Bob asks for a Value by its hash. Every chunk is checked against that hash as it arrives, so nobody can slip in a wrong byte. He can ask for just a range, and from several devices at once.

slides.title: News travels by gossip.
slides.text: When Alice changes the list, her device tells the peers interested in it: “house-list has something new.” They pass it on, and whoever wants it fetches the new sealed chunks.

slides.title: Who may even get the bytes?
slides.text: Read decides who can open data. Three more things a rule can allow decide who can carry it: want, keep and sync. Carriers never see the rules themselves: those are sealed for readers. Whoever asks shows their own proof.
list: want: may ask for this data and receive it, sealed.
keep: may store it for good.
sync: may pass it on to others whose rules say want.

slides.title: want
slides.text: Before a device sends anything, even sealed chunks, the asker shows a proof that a rule gives them {want}. The carrier checks the signatures and nothing else. A stranger gets nothing at all, not even ciphertext to count or keep. Read includes want.

slides.title: keep
slides.text: Your backup gets want and {keep}. It holds every sealed chunk, for good, and gives them back to your new phone. It has no read, so to it they're just sealed bytes.

slides.title: sync
slides.text: The street's always-on peer gets {sync}. It passes your changes between Alice and Bob when they're never online at the same time. It keeps them only as long as it has to.

slides.title: All the rules on one list.
slides.text: One piece of data, one owner, three roles, each with exactly what it needs.

slides.title: Alice and Bob, never online together.
slides.text: Alice ticks milk on the train and goes offline. The street's peer picks it up, the backup keeps it, and Bob's laptop gets it in the evening. Neither carrier read a word.

slides.title: Between devices, in short.
list: Every device's address is its key.
Devices connect directly, or through a relay that sees only sealed traffic.
Docs swap missing sealed chunks; Values stream checked chunks; gossip spreads the news.
want, keep and sync decide who may carry data. Read decides who may open it.
